strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: replacing the common linear scale-and-shift correction of MDE outputs with a learned polynomial transformation, illustrated intuitively via Fig. 1 and the inflection-point argument in Sec. 3.1/3.3.

Extensive empirical evaluation across three datasets (nuScenes, ZJU-4DRadarCam, View-of-Delft) at multiple evaluation distances, with consistent and substantial improvements over five recent radar-camera baselines.

Useful ablations: polynomial degree sensitivity (Tab. 3) showing a clear sweet spot and degradation from over-fitting at very high degree, and component ablations (prototypes, cross-modal fusion, monotonicity loss) that support the design choices.

The monotonicity/first-derivative regularization is a reasonable and lightweight way to constrain an otherwise unconstrained high-degree polynomial fit, and its removal is shown empirically to hurt performance.

Reasonable generality check by testing the approach with four different MDE backbones (DPT, Depth Anything, Depth Pro, UniDepth), showing consistent gains over a comparable radar-guided baseline (RadarCam-Depth) in each case.
Efficiency argument (predicting N+1 scalars rather than per-pixel corrections) is sensible given the sparsity of radar returns relative to image resolution.
weaknesses: The predicted polynomial coefficients are global per-image (obtained via a single GAP-pooled scene vector), meaning the depth correction is purely a function of the MDE-predicted depth value z at a pixel, not of pixel location; the paper's motivating narrative about correcting cross-object/spatial misalignments is therefore only valid to the extent that the misplaced objects already differ in their raw MDE depth values, which is not explicitly analyzed or discussed as a boundary condition of the method.

Polynomials are known to be poorly behaved under extrapolation (Runge's phenomenon); the monotonicity term is only a soft, average, L1-penalized regularizer rather than a hard constraint, so there is no guarantee against non-monotonic or unstable behavior for depth values outside the distribution seen during training, and this risk is not empirically probed (e.g., via extrapolation stress tests).

The polynomial degree is an important hyperparameter that reportedly needs per-dataset tuning (acknowledged as a limitation in one sentence), yet the paper provides no protocol or guidance for selecting it on new data, nor an ablation on how sensitive the model is to this choice across datasets/backbones beyond nuScenes and ZJU.

The magnitude of improvement varies widely across datasets (11.3% nuScenes vs. 54.6% ZJU vs. 35.2% VoD per the abstract's contribution list), which could reflect dataset-specific overfitting of the polynomial degree or architecture rather than a uniformly generalizable gain; no cross-dataset generalization experiment (e.g., train on one dataset, test on another) is reported.

Limited discussion of failure cases or negative results; the Limitations section is very brief (two sentences) and does not address the spatial-invariance issue above, extrapolation risk, or sensitivity to radar sparsity/noise beyond qualitative claims.

Details needed for reproducibility (training protocol, hyperparameters λ1–λ3, architecture dimensions, number of prototypes NP, exact backbone freezing/fine-tuning setup, baseline retraining details) are deferred to supplementary material not included in the review, making it hard to fully judge fairness of baseline comparisons and reproducibility from the main text alone.

No reported computational cost/parameter-count comparison against baselines in the main paper (only a qualitative claim of “negligible overhead”), and no variance/multiple-run statistics are provided for the main results.

strengths: The core idea—replacing a global scale-and-shift correction with a polynomial function of the MDE-predicted depth value—is intuitive and well-motivated conceptually, and the paper provides a reasonable geometric narrative (inflection points, curvature) for why higher-order corrections could help with cross-region depth misalignment.

The monotonicity regularization via first-derivative penalty is a sensible mechanism to counteract a known failure mode of high-degree polynomial fitting (oscillation/order-reversal), and its ablation (Table 4) shows it contributes measurably to performance.

The empirical evaluation spans three datasets (nuScenes, ZJU-4DRadarCam, View-of-Delft) at multiple evaluation distances, and includes comparisons against several fairly recent radar-camera depth baselines as well as ablations over MDE backbones (Table 2) and polynomial degree (Table 3).
Qualitative visualizations (Figs. 3-4) are provided to illustrate the claimed mechanism of correcting cross-object misalignment, and the writing/motivation in Sections 1 and 3.1 is reasonably clear.
weaknesses: A single set of N+1 polynomial coefficients is predicted per image and applied uniformly to the entire scaleless depth map (Eq. 1/7). This means the correction for any pixel depends only on its scalar MDE depth value z, not its spatial location or local context. Two spatially separated, semantically distinct regions that happen to share the same predicted MDE depth value receive identical corrections. This directly undercuts the paper's central narrative about correcting misalignment between local object regions that MDE places at incorrect relative depths (Fig. 1)—if two misaligned objects have similar raw MDE depth values, a purely value-based polynomial cannot distinguish or correct them differently. This fundamental architectural limitation is never explicitly acknowledged or analyzed.

No discussion or ablation addresses numerical stability of exponentiating raw depth values (up to 80m) to powers as high as 8 or 10 (Table 3). Without explicit normalization details (not stated in the paper), z^8 for z≈80 would be astronomically large, which is either a major omission in the presentation or hints at unreported preprocessing that should have been specified for reproducibility.

The best polynomial degree is treated as a per-dataset tuned hyperparameter (Table 3), which the authors themselves list as a limitation. This weakens the generality of the 'principled' claim and suggests the method requires dataset-specific tuning to reach reported SOTA numbers, raising concerns about how the specific degree (8) reported as default throughout the main results was selected/validated (e.g., whether test-set information influenced this choice).

The monotonicity constraint is only a soft regularizer (average derivative near 1) and does not guarantee monotonicity; especially at high polynomial degree, local order reversals remain possible in regions away from where the loss is minimized, which is inconsistent with the safety-critical framing (e.g., navigation) motivating the paper.

The magnitude of improvement over RadarCam-Depth (30-60% MAE/RMSE reduction across datasets, e.g., ZJU 46.8%/62.4%) is very large given that RadarCam-Depth already uses a similar MDE+radar scale-fitting paradigm. Without reported variance across seeds/runs, statistical significance testing, or clear confirmation that baselines were reproduced/tuned under matched conditions (backbone, training data splits, hyperparameters), it is hard to assess whether these gains reflect the polynomial-fitting idea itself versus other confounds (e.g., backbone choice, training recipe differences).

The RMSE at 80m on VoD degrades sharply relative to 50m/70m (2420→2803→3952), a proportionally larger increase than most baselines exhibit, which is consistent with instability of high-degree polynomial extrapolation beyond the depth range seen during training/fitting—a concern the paper does not discuss despite claiming the method is robust and well-posed.

The architectural contribution (learnable prototypes + cross-attention fusion between radar and depth features) is a fairly standard transformer-style cross-attention/pooling design; its novelty is incremental relative to existing radar-camera fusion literature, and the paper's claims of being a fundamentally new paradigm partly rest on this component as much as on the polynomial-fitting idea.
No confidence intervals, multiple-seed results, or significance tests are reported for any table, which is a material gap given the very large claimed margins over prior SOTA.

The claim of being the 'first' to apply polynomial fitting to adapt foundation model predictions is a strong originality claim that is not rigorously substantiated against the broader literature on non-linear scale correction/calibration methods outside the specific radar-depth niche cited.

strengths: The central idea—replacing a global linear scale-and-shift correction with a learned polynomial function of the MDE-predicted depth—is simple, well-motivated, and clearly explained with intuitive geometric arguments (inflection points, curvature) and an informative illustrative figure (Fig. 1, Fig. 4).

Strong and consistent empirical gains are shown across three distinct datasets (nuScenes, ZJU-4DRadarCam, View-of-Delft) and three evaluation distances (50/70/80m), with sizeable margins over five recent radar-camera depth completion/fusion baselines (Table 1).

The MDE-backbone comparison (Table 2) demonstrates that the polynomial-fitting idea generalizes across four different pretrained MDE models (DPT, Depth Anything, Depth Pro, UniDepth), which strengthens the claim that the improvement stems from the proposed transformation rather than from a specific backbone.

The ablation studies (Tables 3 and 4) are reasonably thorough, examining the sensitivity to polynomial degree and isolating the contributions of the learnable prototypes, cross-modality attention, and the monotonicity regularizer.

The proposed first-derivative monotonicity regularization is a sensible and lightweight mechanism to prevent overfitting/oscillation that could otherwise arise from higher-degree polynomial fits, and it is shown empirically to help (Table 4).

The method is architecturally simple relative to prior multi-stage radar-camera fusion pipelines, and the authors argue (with some justification) that the added computational overhead over a linear scale-and-shift model is minimal.
weaknesses: A single set of polynomial coefficients is predicted per scene (via global-average-pooling over the fused representation before the coefficient MLP), meaning the final correction is a fixed function purely of the scalar MDE-predicted depth value z(x,y) at each pixel. Consequently, any two pixels/objects that the MDE model places at the *same* predicted depth—even if their true depths differ—cannot be disambiguated by any polynomial (or even more complex) function of z alone. The motivating example in Fig. 1 implicitly assumes the MDE's ordinal/relative errors are separable by depth value, but this assumption is never stated or examined, leaving a gap between the stated motivation (arbitrary cross-object misalignment) and what the method can actually correct.

The claim that the number of polynomial degrees of freedom "empirically... [is] close to the cardinality of radar point clouds" is asserted but not rigorously derived or tested; it reads as post-hoc justification rather than a principled design choice, and no analysis relates polynomial degree to the number of radar points across the three datasets, which differ considerably in radar density.

The optimal polynomial degree is dataset-dependent and must be tuned as a hyperparameter (acknowledged as a limitation by the authors), yet no guidance, adaptive scheme, or validation procedure for selecting it is proposed beyond grid search results in Table 3, which limits practical reproducibility.

In the ablation study (Table 4), removing cross-modality attention causes a very large performance drop (roughly 50% relative increase in error), noticeably larger than removing other components; it is unclear exactly what this ablated variant replaces the fusion mechanism with (e.g., naive concatenation vs. no radar signal at all), and this detail is not specified in the main text, making it hard to judge whether the comparison is fair or whether the fallback is a weak baseline by construction.

Key implementation and training details (loss weights λ1, λ2, λ3, number of prototypes NP, radar/depth feature dimensionalities, training schedule, number of parameters, and runtime/latency numbers) are deferred to supplementary material not included here, limiting the ability to fully assess reproducibility and efficiency claims from the main text alone.

The paper does not report variance across multiple training runs or any statistical significance testing for the reported improvements, nor does it include failure-case analysis for PolyRad itself (only qualitative comparisons where PolyRad outperforms baselines are shown), which limits assessment of robustness.

The related-work distinction from prior scale-and-shift or affine correction methods is reasonably made, but the sweeping claim that "no prior work has explored polynomial fitting for adapting predictions of pretrained foundation models" is a strong, essentially unverifiable statement that would benefit from more tempered phrasing given the breadth of literature on model calibration/post-hoc correction in other domains.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: extending scale-and-shift affine correction of MDE outputs to a higher-degree polynomial transformation, with an intuitive geometric argument (inflection points) for why affine correction fails when 3+ misaligned regions are present.

Extensive empirical validation across three datasets (nuScenes, ZJU-4DRadarCam, View-of-Delft) against a reasonably comprehensive set of recent baselines (RadarNet, SparseBeatsDense, GET-UP, RadarCam-Depth, TacoDepth), with both accuracy and efficiency (latency, GFLOPs, training time) reported.

Thorough ablation studies covering polynomial degree sensitivity, architectural components (learnable prototypes, cross-modal fusion, monotonicity loss, positional embeddings), MDE backbone swapping (4 backbones tested), zero-shot cross-dataset generalization, robustness to reduced radar density, and comparisons against alternative regression/adapter baselines (isotonic regression, splines, LoRA, ViT-Adapter).

The first-derivative monotonicity regularization is a sensible design choice to constrain the expressive polynomial space, and its benefit is supported both by an ablation and by a Kendall's tau monotonicity analysis with a statistical significance test.
Strong efficiency profile (real-time ~40 fps, lowest GFLOPs and training time among compared methods) makes the method practically attractive if the accuracy claims hold.
weaknesses: Appendix H's 'Proposition 1' and accompanying 'proof' are essentially a restatement of basic linear algebra (three generic points are not exactly collinear), yet are presented with formal theorem/corollary framing that overstates the theoretical contribution of the paper.

The claimed magnitude of improvement varies drastically and inconsistently across datasets (e.g., ~4% MAE reduction on nuScenes vs. ~38-58% on ZJU and VoD), and the strongest baseline (TacoDepth) is missing entirely from the VoD comparison, which weakens the claim of consistent state-of-the-art performance across all three datasets and makes the headline aggregate percentages (24.9%/33.2% in the abstract vs. 29.1% in the introduction) somewhat inconsistent and possibly cherry-picked in presentation.

The method raises the scaleless MDE depth z to high powers (up to degree 8 or 10 per the sensitivity study) without any described normalization or numerical conditioning strategy; given real depth ranges up to 50-80m, z^8 could produce extreme dynamic range and potential optimization instability, but this practical concern is not discussed or ablated.

The optimal polynomial degree is dataset-dependent and must be tuned as a hyperparameter (explicitly acknowledged as a limitation), which undercuts the claim of a principled, generalizable solution and raises concerns about overfitting to each benchmark's characteristics.

Some qualitative and interpretability claims (e.g., sign of polynomial coefficients corresponding to over/under-estimation correction, Fig. 3 narrative) are illustrated anecdotally on individual examples rather than validated systematically.

No discussion of code/model release or detailed reproducibility artifacts beyond stated hyperparameters, limiting independent verification of the pipeline (radar prototype learning, fusion module specifics, training schedule nuances).

strengths: Clear, well-motivated core idea: replacing the ubiquitous global affine (scale-and-shift) correction of MDE outputs with a learned polynomial transformation is a simple but underexplored generalization, and the paper gives good geometric intuition (inflection points) for why affine correction is insufficient when 3+ regions are misplaced relative to each other.

The first-derivative (approximate monotonicity) regularizer is a sensible and lightweight way to control the otherwise large hypothesis space introduced by high-degree polynomials, and its necessity is empirically supported (Table 6 ablation, Kendall's tau analysis in Appendix G).

Extensive empirical validation: three datasets (nuScenes, ZJU-4DRadarCam, VoD), multiple MDE backbones (DPT, Depth Anything, Depth Pro, UniDepth), sensitivity study over polynomial degree, ablations of architectural components, zero-shot cross-dataset transfer, robustness to radar point sparsification, and comparisons against lidar-completion baselines (NLSPN, BPNet) and generic regression/adapter baselines (isotonic regression, splines, LoRA, ViT-Adapter).

Strong and consistent efficiency gains (lowest training time, lowest inference latency, lowest GFLOPs) alongside accuracy improvements, which is a meaningful practical contribution for real-time deployment scenarios.
The paper is transparent about limitations (degree as a dataset-dependent hyperparameter) and provides a reasonably detailed method description with FLOP-level efficiency analysis.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification in Appendix H (Proposition 1) is essentially a restatement of the fact that 3 arbitrary/noisy points generally cannot be fit by a 2-parameter affine model; this is true of almost any noisy 3-point set and does not specifically justify why a polynomial (versus any other flexible nonlinear/piecewise model) is the right or best-motivated correction, nor does it bound how much a high-degree polynomial actually needs to correct in practice. The "proof" reads as an appeal to intuition rather than substantive theoretical support.

Numerical stability of raising raw scaleless depth values to high powers (up to degree 8-10) is not discussed. Since scaleless MDE outputs and metric depths can span tens of meters, z^8 terms could span many orders of magnitude, and the paper does not explain any normalization/rescaling of z before exponentiation, which is a plausible practical concern for training stability that is not addressed.

The architectural novelty is somewhat incremental: prototype-based soft clustering for point cloud aggregation and cross-attention-based multimodal fusion are established techniques (adapted from other point-cloud/depth-completion literature); the core contribution is really the polynomial output head and the monotonicity loss, which is comparatively narrow.

Selection of the polynomial degree as a hyperparameter that must be tuned per-dataset (as acknowledged) somewhat undercuts the claimed simplicity/efficiency advantage over more complex architectures, and no principled or automatic method for choosing degree is proposed.

Baseline comparisons, while broad, are all recent point estimates from other papers' reported numbers (or re-implementations); some experimental details (e.g., identical train/test protocol, exact backbone matching) are not fully specified, making it hard to fully verify apples-to-apples comparison, particularly for latency/FLOPs numbers reported for competing methods.
